prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock, which made atomic frequency standards accurate to about one part in 10^18 and opened new precision tests of fundamental physics

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a single, clearly stated idea (trap many atoms in a lattice at the magic wavelength, so the light shift cancels and Doppler and recoil effects vanish) that was followed by a decisive demonstration of its power. It has been reproduced and pushed by several independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, SYRTE, PTB, NIST) and the interpretation is stable. It lets us see time inside atoms at a level that was unimaginable twenty years ago: gravitational redshift over millimetres, searches for variation of constants and dark-matter couplings, many-body effects in the clock itself. Four of the five members who ranked B022 put Katori and Ye together, and the attribution is the tightest on the list. Recognition is timely, with the redefinition of the second under discussion, and little risk of being premature.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with earlier prizes: Hall and Hansch (2005) for the frequency comb that makes the clocks possible, and Wineland (2012) for single-ion control and ion clocks. A sceptic can say that lattice clocks are the next step in a lineage already honoured, and a measurement tool rather than a discovery about nature, which cuts against my own taste for the unexpected. Priority is not fully clean either: Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley and the ion-clock groups (Wineland, Hall) are not in the credit, and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the lattice clock second, but notes overlap with the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, and that the lattice-versus-single-ion claim to foundational credit is not settled.
responses.response: I take the overlap seriously, but it does not weaken B022 as much as it first seems. The comb is the ruler and the 2012 work concerns control of single quantum systems; neither contains the magic-wavelength idea, which is what allows millions of atoms to be interrogated at once without perturbation. That is why the best single-ion clocks have not reached the same stability. I accept that the citation must be written carefully so it names the lattice concept and not clocks generally. I would not accept that this makes it a lesser candidate than the gamma-ray burst afterglow entry that you place first.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B022 first as a textbook measurement that moves the limit of what can be observed, with multiple independent labs and a clean two-name attribution, while noting that boundaries against Hall and Wineland-era clock work need care.
responses.response: I agree on the scientific case and on the two names, and we are on the same side as experimentalist-minded readers of a systematic budget. I would qualify one point: we should not let our shared enthusiasm for precision stand in for breadth of impact. The case is strongest if we stress the new physics it exposes, such as redshift on millimetre scales, many-body clock physics and constant-variation bounds. I would also like us to check that Katori's early strontium demonstration and Ye's accuracy record are both needed in the citation; if one is doubtful, the two-person claim becomes less obvious.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators first as a new class of quantum matter with protected edge and surface states, a clear theory-experiment loop, independently confirmed for about twenty years, and a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio that is defensible but not uncontested.
responses.response: I agree that B039 is a genuine organising principle, and it was my own second choice for that reason. My difficulty is attribution, not merit. Your own ballot lists Bernevig, Zhang, Hasan, Moore and Balents as missing, and the HgTe experiment followed Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang directly. Within a three-name limit I cannot see how to give Kane, Mele and Molenkamp the whole field without telling a story that the people we leave out would dispute. I would therefore keep B039 as my first alternative. If you can argue that the 2D quantum spin Hall effect alone is a cleanly bounded achievement, so that the 3D work is a separate matter, I would be willing to move it up. Condensed matter is not my field, so I would defer to you on that.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as a new regime of single-photon coupling that underlies superconducting processors, and also ranks trapped-ion computing second, while declaring proximity to the superconducting-circuit community.
responses.response: I value both arguments, and I appreciate the open declaration of your ties. For B023 my worry is timing: the 2025 prize recognised macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, and giving the field a further prize this soon looks to me like too narrow a focus, with Girvin and Devoret leaving real gaps in the credited names. On B005 I largely agree with your ranking of Cirac, Zoller and Blatt as a strong idea followed by sustained experiment, and that is why I keep it as an alternative. My reservation is the 2012 overlap and the unresolved experimental credit to Monroe and the NIST group, which a Blatt-only experimental credit does not settle.

uncertainties: Whether colleagues treat the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes as leaving room for a precision-timekeeping prize, or as already covering the lineage.
Whether the citation can credit Katori and Ye without implicitly undervaluing Lemonde, Ludlow and others, and without overlap in wording with earlier prizes.
Whether the redefinition of the second, still pending, should be awaited; I think not, because the science is already settled.
I rely on my own knowledge of the magic-wavelength priority history and have not independently verified it in this round.
statement.conflict_note: Specific connection: I have an attosecond-physics and atomic-theory collaboration with the Lund group of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate), but none of the B022 candidates (Katori, Ye) appears in my profile as a collaborator or institutional colleague. I have co-authored with the Lund and ETH attosecond groups and Reinhold Schuch, none of whom are credited on this shortlist. I do not find a specific conflict for B022, B039 or B005 from the provided profile; Cirac, Zoller and Blatt are not in my listed connections.
